idiom_name: foldLeft / foldRight / fold / reduceOption on Scala collections
implementation_notes: Scala's collections define the fold on IterableOnceOps: foldLeft[B](z: B)(op: (B, A) => B) applies the operator left to right, foldRight applies it from the last element, fold(z)(op) and reduce/reduceOption are the usual companions, and the deprecated /: and :\ operators are documented as foldLeft/foldRight spellings (the docs advise foldLeft for sequential collections). The API documents the boundary of the strict forms: folds will not terminate for infinite-sized collections, and a stdlib foldRight on a long lazy structure can build the whole chain before combining, which is why the cats variant exists. For a recursive type the fold is hand-written over a sealed hierarchy with a match, or derived by a recursion-schemes library.
code_sketch:
val total = orders.foldLeft(0L)((acc, o) => acc + o.amount)
val rendered = List(1, 2, 3).foldRight("end")((v, acc) => s"($v $acc)")

val same = List(1, 2, 3).sum                    // monoid specialization
val maybe = List[Int]().reduceOption(_ + _)     // None instead of an exception
pitfalls: foldRight on a lazy or very long structure defeats laziness: the standard library's foldRight is not the Eval-based lazy fold (cats provides foldr for that), and the docs warn that folds do not terminate on infinite collections.

foldLeft and foldRight disagree for non-associative operations, and the accumulator type is inferred from the seed, so a wrongly typed seed silently selects a different carrier or fails to compile in a confusing place.
reduce/reduceLeft on an empty collection throw UnsupportedOperationException, so emptiness must be handled with reduceOption or a fold with an explicit identity.

variants.name: cats Foldable: lazy foldRight with Eval and foldMap over a Monoid
variants.implementation_notes: cats abstracts folding into a type class: Foldable[F] is implemented in terms of foldLeft and a lazy foldRight whose signature is foldRight(fa, lb: Eval[B])(f: (A, Eval[B]) => Eval[B]) - the Eval wrapper is what lets short-circuiting folds (exists/forall/find) terminate on infinite structures where the stdlib foldRight runs out of memory. foldMap needs only a Monoid for the carrier and an instance for the container, which is the Fold/Catamorphism in its monoid form, and fold/foldK fold a structure of monoids into one. Choose it when the code is already written against cats' type classes or when laziness matters; for a concrete collection a plain foldLeft carries no dependency.
variants.code_sketch:
import cats._
import cats.syntax.all._

val joined: String = Foldable[List].foldMap(List(1, 2, 4))(_.toString)    // "124"
val sum: Int       = Foldable[List].fold(List(1, 2, 3))                    // Monoid[Int]

// the lazy foldRight short-circuits where the stdlib would run out of memory:
val res: Boolean = Foldable[LazyList]
  .foldRight(LazyList.continually(false), Eval.True)((a, acc) => if (a) acc else Eval.False)
  .value                                                                   // false
pitfalls: cats' lazy foldRight clashes with the collection's own foldRight of the same name, which is why the alias foldr exists - and a wildcard cats.syntax import can silently change which overload a call resolves to.

foldMap demands an implicit Monoid and an implicit Foldable: a missing instance is a compile error, but an incoherent Monoid (a non-associative combine) is accepted and quietly breaks the laws the type class assumes.

Eval-based folds retain what they have not forced: a lazy foldRight over a large LazyList still holds the unevaluated thunks if the structure stays reachable, so laziness trades memory rather than removing it.

variants.name: Recursion schemes: cata over a fixed point (droste / Matryoshka)
variants.idiom_name: base functor + Fix + library-provided cata (algebras and scheme zoo)
variants.implementation_notes: The literal catamorphism: describe one layer of the structure as a base functor, take its fixed point, and let the library's cata fold a Recursive structure with an algebra F[A] => A, so the traversal is derived instead of written per data type. droste (recursion schemes for cats) exposes algebras and coalgebras and a scheme zoo (scheme.zoo.cata, dyna, and the general ghylo), and Matryoshka is its credited predecessor; the payoff is the derived family (cata, para, zygo, histo, hylo) and the laws that travel with it, and the price is a heavyweight encoding - functor instances, Fix, higher-kinded types and type lambdas in every signature. Select it for compiler-style data types where several schemes over the same shape are genuinely needed; a plain foldLeft is a better answer for a list.
pitfalls: The encoding is infectious: Fix, a Functor instance per layer, higher-kinded type lambdas and the library's Algebra/Coalgebra wrappers appear in every signature, and the readability cost is paid even where a plain fold would do.

cata is bottom-up and total: it cannot stop early, and the algebra sees only the folded children, never the original child node (that needs a paramorphism or zygomorphism), so search-style and context-sensitive traversals need a different scheme.

The libraries live outside the Scala distribution (droste is community-maintained, Matryoshka is its legacy predecessor), so adopting recursion schemes adds a dependency whose maintenance and Scala-version alignment must be weighed against the derived schemes.
